newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN GOVT, WINE INDUSTRY LOCK HORNS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN GOVT, WINE INDUSTRY LOCK HORNS.

text.p: The South African government on Thursday locked horns with the country's wine industry when Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom moved to delay powerful wine co-operative KWV's bid to become a private company.
At stake was a court application by KWV to change its status from a statutory co-operative while remaining the regulatory body for the industry.

Analysts have been incensed by the co-operative's bid to privatise assets worth about two billion rand built up over years of stifling control by KWV over the wine industry, with the help of special tax breaks granted to it as a statuory body.

Hanekom, who had set up a special task team to investigate the move announced by KWV chairman Lourens Jonker in October, is understood to have been equally concerned about the fact that the KWV was both referee and player in the wine industry and now wanted to privatise its regulatory function.
Despite intense behind-the-scenes negotiations in recent weeks, KWV on Thursday went ahead with its application to be declared a private company by the end of April.
Hanekom responded by saying that he, in turn, would apply for a court order to delay KWV's plans until he had satisfied himself that this was in the best interests of the industry.
In the end, the two parties agreed that their applications should be postponed until March 25, with each side having the right to file further papers in support of their case.
Analysts welcomed the intervention by Hanekom, saying that there should first be a thorough assessment of KWV's assets and how they were obtained as well as its future regulatory role.
Leading wine analyst Michael Fridjhon said that Hanekom "did the right thing" by insisting that he had the right to take "a long hard look at the implications" of privatisation.
But KWV chairman Lourens Jonker said that KWV's assets were the inalienable property of its 4,751 wine farmer members.
"Any actions by the state to the contrary could be construed as an act of nationalisation," Jonker said.
Analysts also believe that the court battle provides an ideal opportunity to redefine KWV's regulatory role.
Until recently, KWV issued quotas limiting the production of wine grapes and it still has the final say over whether farmers can make wine.
Fridjhon said that KWV had favoured farmers producing distilling wine at the expense of the few hundred quality wine-makers who were making their mark in world wine markets.

Jonker said that KWV's statutory powers could be exercised in partnership with the producing wholesale trade and the state but analysts believe that a completely independant regulatory authoirity is now needed.
